nodes.title: Chain Theory
nodes.subtitle: Only entangled pairs exist
nodes.size: Below all lengths (space is built later)
summary: A new idea by Alex Wissner-Gross (Oct 2026).
Reality = networks of linked tiny quantum units.
Brand new. Not yet tested by others.
details: ## Alex says
"Nothing exists but finitely many maximally entangled pairs of qudits, some qudits shared, known only by distilling them."
That one sentence is the only input. Alex aims for "no free parameters".
Particles would be "chainmail": finite meshes of these links. "A chain, not a string."
## Our reading
It is like a building made only of linked rings. Everything else is how the rings join.
deeper: A compendium of 100 theorems, 109 conditional theorems and 198 open results (release 0.1).
"Theorem" here often means a check over a finite list of networks, not a proof for all.
That its pieces ARE real physics is called a conjecture by Alex himself.
Peer review. Independent checks. A second number that matches a measurement.
Posted 23–24 Oct 2026, so only days old. No independent review found yet (checked 26 Oct 2026).
Made with a "human-superintelligence collaboration". The author has a financial interest in Physical Superintelligence PBC.

nodes.title: Quantum fields
nodes.subtitle: Standard Model: tested
summary: Every particle is a ripple in a field.
The Standard Model: 17 particles, 3 forces.
Tested extremely precisely.
details: ## Recipe
12 matter fields (6 quarks, 6 leptons) + force fields (gluons, photon, W, Z) + the Higgs field.
## How it works
A field is spread over all space. A ripple of fixed size is a particle.
The rules come from symmetry: SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1).
deeper: Its predictions match experiments, e.g. the electron's magnetism to about 1 part in a trillion.
About 19–26 constants must be measured (masses, strengths). The theory does not explain them.
No gravity. No dark matter. Why 3 generations? Why these masses?

Its gravity results are all graded "open" (Open result 1.9).

nodes.title: Qudits & pairs
nodes.subtitle: The links of the chain
summary: A qudit is a tiny quantum unit with d states.
Two qudits share one perfect entangled state.
That pair is one "link".
details: ## Alex says
A qudit has dimension 2 or more (2 = qubit, 3 = qutrit).
A pair is "maximally entangled": as linked as quantum rules allow.
A shared qudit is the end of 2+ pairs. It carries one copy per pair (because entanglement is "monogamous").
## Recipe
2 qudits → 1 link. Links join at shared qudits → a network.
deeper: A less-than-perfect pair would need smooth, continuous numbers. A fully discrete theory cannot have them.
Monogamy of entanglement and tensor networks (PEPS) are standard quantum information.
That reality is made ONLY of these pairs is the untested part.

nodes.title: Distillation
nodes.subtitle: "To know is to link"
summary: To look at a link, you distill it.
Distilling 2 qudits makes them a new pair.
Time = a count of these acts.
details: ## Alex says
To distill two qudits is to project them onto a perfect pair. One copy, no failure.
A "read" is a distillation at one end of a pair.
What is "known" is only what reads can fix with certainty.
## Like
Entanglement swapping: link 1–2 and 3–4, distill 2 with 3, and now 1–4 is a pair.
deeper: "Time is counted, not assumed." Graded a conditional theorem (box 50.1).
The usual quantum probability rule comes out as an output (Alex grades it conditional).
Entanglement swapping is a real lab effect (since 1998).

nodes.title: Six kinds of link
nodes.subtitle: Only 2 can be read
summary: Links are typed by end sizes: (2,2), (3,2)…

details: ## Alex says
Ends have dimension 2, 3 or 4 ("Conjecture 0", a conditional theorem).
A link is readable when d₁×d₂ ≤ 6 (math of Størmer, Woronowicz, Choi).

(2,2) spacetime · (3,2) photon / electromagnetism · (4,2) weak force · (3,3) strong force · (4,3) Yukawa (mass) · (4,4) Higgs.
deeper: The 6 genres and the read cap are derived. Which physics each one IS: conjectured, some matched only "by name" (Alex’s words).

nodes.title: Forces from one link
nodes.subtitle: Qutrit + qubit symmetry
summary: A qutrit linked to a qubit has a symmetry.
It is the same shape as the Standard Model's.
A striking match. Meaning not yet proven.
details: ## Alex says
Turning the qutrit end gives SU(3). Turning the qubit end gives SU(2). One shared phase gives U(1).
Together: (SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1))/ℤ₆, the exact group of the Standard Model.
Its charge is the hypercharge with Y = 1/6, like the left-handed quark doublet.
deeper: The group S(U(3)×U(2)) ≅ (SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1))/ℤ₆ is known (Baez & Huerta 2010).
Alex's new step is reading it as the symmetry of ONE entangled pair.
Why this pair and not others? How hypercharge becomes electric charge is "beyond the Letter".

nodes.title: Hot Big Bang
nodes.subtitle: Hot, dense, expanding
nodes.size: Today's visible universe was once tiny
summary: 13.8 billion years ago.
Hot, dense, and expanding ever since.
Seen in the afterglow light.
details: ## What it is
Not an explosion in space. Space itself stretching, everywhere.
## Timeline
10⁻¹² s: forces split. 10⁻⁵ s: protons form. 3 min: first nuclei. 380,000 yr: atoms.
deeper: Galaxies move apart (Hubble). The afterglow (CMB). The right amounts of H, He, Li.

nodes.title: Higgs field
nodes.subtitle: Gives tiny particles mass
summary: Its particle was found in 2012.
It gives quarks, electrons, W and Z their mass.
NOT most of YOUR mass (see protons).
details: ## How it gives mass
Particles get mass by coupling to the field's steady value (246 GeV) everywhere in space.
## The numbers
Higgs boson: 125.2 GeV (PDG 2024). Found by ATLAS and CMS at CERN, 4 July 2012.
deeper: Only ~1% of a proton's mass comes from Higgs-given quark masses. ~99% is strong-force energy.
Why these couplings? Is the vacuum stable? Do neutrinos get mass this way? Unknown.
Alex conjectures the Higgs is a "closed hub read" in (4,4) links (conditional).

nodes.title: Chainmail particles
nodes.subtitle: Particles as webs of links
summary: Each particle = a small web of links.
Its insides can't be pulled apart by collisions.
So it looks like a point. Alex's idea.
details: ## Alex says
Particles have no visible parts because their parts are "undistillable", not too small.
Example, the electron web: 9 sites and 10 links. A core triangle of three (3,3) links plus one "hub assembly" (links of types (4,2), (3,2), (4,3), (2,2)).
Muon and tau add more hubs to the same core (the tau is "the third hub on the triangle core"). Alex reads this as 3 generations (conditional 152.1).
## Recipe
Links + shared qudits → closed webs.
deeper: 17 particles drawn on 16 webs: 1 on a theorem, 11 conditional, 2 open, 3 not yet in the release.
"That a web is the named particle is a conjecture."
A neat idea: like knots in chainmail. No mass or charge of a real particle has been derived from a web yet (Thm 176.1).
Prediction: no 4th generation. Fits LEP's count of 3 light neutrinos.

nodes.title: Space & time from links?
nodes.subtitle: (2,2) links → spacetime
summary: Alex: space and time are not given.

Spacetime has 1 time + 3 space directions: "one against three" (a theorem of the networks).
Gravity is "a statement about counting": a metric from the depth of a web, curvature as a graph Laplacian (conditional).
A cosmological term (dark energy?) at the "depth exponent" (conditional).
deeper: "Spacetime from entanglement" (Van Raamsdonk 2010) and gravity from thermodynamics (Jacobson 1995) are real research lines.
No measured gravity number (like G) is derived yet. Much of Part VI (metric, worldline, horizon) is conditional or open.

Photons stop bumping into free electrons → fly freely.

summary: Ageing Sun-like giants catch neutrons slowly.
Makes about half the elements past iron.
E.g. barium, lead, strontium.

Nucleus + 1 neutron at a time (years between catches) → heavier, then beta-decay.
In stars of ~1–8 Sun masses (AGB stars).

Up to lead and bismuth.

nodes.title: Fusion in stars
nodes.subtitle: H → He → C, O … → Fe
summary: 4 H → 1 He, in all stars.
3 He → 1 C, then O, Ne, Si…
Up to iron in big stars.
details: ## Recipes
4 protons → 1 helium-4 + 26.7 MeV (0.7% of mass becomes energy).
3 helium-4 → carbon-12 at ~100 million K.
C + He → O. Then Ne, Mg, Si, S… Silicon → iron at ~3 billion K.
## Why stop at iron
Iron/nickel have the most tightly-bound nuclei. Fusing further costs energy.
deeper: Exact rate of C + He → O is still uncertain; it sets how much O vs C we get.

nodes.title: Cosmic-ray splitting
nodes.subtitle: Makes Li, Be, B

details: ## Recipe
Fast proton + carbon/oxygen nucleus → smaller pieces.
deeper: Li, Be, B are ~10⁵–10⁷× rarer than C and O; the amounts match cosmic-ray models.

Star > ~8 Sun masses + iron core ~1.4 Suns → collapse → explosion.
~99% of the energy leaves as neutrinos (seen for SN 1987A).
deeper: Exactly how the blast restarts is still modelled, not fully solved.

nodes.title: White-dwarf blasts
nodes.subtitle: Type Ia: makes iron

details: ## Recipe
White dwarf near 1.4 Sun masses (or two merging) → thermonuclear blast.
deeper: Which path (gaining gas, or a merger) is most common is debated.

Neutron flood makes gold, platinum, uranium.

2 neutron stars (~1.4 Suns each, ~20 km wide) → kilonova.

nodes.title: String theory
nodes.subtitle: Rival: tiny vibrating strings
nodes.size: Strings near the Planck length (~10⁻³⁵ m)
summary: Particles = vibrating strings.
Needs extra hidden dimensions.
Rich maths, no test yet.
details: ## The idea
Every particle is one tiny string vibrating in a different way. Gravity comes out automatically.
It needs 10 dimensions (11 in M-theory); the extra ones would be curled up too small to see.
## Where it stands
The biggest quantum-gravity programme. It gave holography (AdS/CFT), a key tool. But it allows a huge number of possible universes, so it has not picked out ours.
deeper: No experiment has seen strings, extra dimensions or supersymmetry (LHC so far).

virtual_cell.title: Typical human cell (generalised)
summary: A general human body cell, about 20 µm across: it has the parts most human cells share.
No single real cell type looks exactly like this; the shape is simplified.
details: Real human cells range from about 7 µm (red blood cells) to over 100 µm, and from round to long and branched.
Sizes and speeds of the parts inside are real measured values, drawn to scale.
Some counts are reduced so you can see between things: proteins at ~1/8 of real crowding, 30 of ~10,000 vaults, fewer microtubules and ribosomes.

virtual_cell.title: Cell membrane
summary: A skin of fat molecules two layers thick, about 5 nm.
It lets some things in and keeps others out.
details: Made of roughly a billion lipid molecules, with proteins floating in it.
In cells that crawl, the front edge ruffles and moves forward a few µm per minute (a lamellipodium).
Zoom right in to see the two layers of lipids.

virtual_cell.title: Nucleus
summary: The control centre: about 10 × 8 µm here (typically 5–10 µm).
It holds 46 chromosomes: about 2 metres of DNA.
details: About 6.2 billion DNA letters (base pairs) in two copies of the genome.
Wrapped in a double membrane with a few thousand pores.
Under a microscope (🔬 button) it glows blue, like the DAPI dye biologists use to stain DNA.

virtual_cell.title: Chromatin (DNA)
summary: DNA wound on protein spools (nucleosomes).
Each spool holds 147 DNA letters, wrapped almost twice.
details: A nucleosome is about 11 nm wide and made of 8 histone proteins.
About 30 million nucleosomes pack the genome into the nucleus.
In living cells the beads fold into irregular chains 5–24 nm wide, not a neat uniform 30 nm fibre.

virtual_cell.title: Nucleosome
summary: A spool of 8 histone proteins with DNA wrapped around it.
About 11 nm wide.
details: 147 base pairs wrap about 1.65 turns.
Linker DNA joins one spool to the next, like beads on a string.
Drawn simplified: DNA wrapped around histone beads. The two twisted strands are the 2 nm double helix; the wrapping around each bead is not drawn.

virtual_cell.title: Nucleolus
summary: A dense spot inside the nucleus, 1–3 µm.
It builds the parts of ribosomes.
details: Most human cells have 1–4. It has no membrane: it forms where ribosome genes cluster.
Ribosome pieces leave through the nuclear pores.

virtual_cell.title: Nuclear pore
summary: A gate in the nucleus wall, about 120 nm across.
mRNA goes out, proteins come in.
details: One of the biggest machines in the cell: ~1,000 proteins of ~30 kinds, in 8-fold symmetry.
A human nucleus has roughly 2,000–5,000 pores.

virtual_cell.title: Ribosome
summary: A protein-building machine, about 25–30 nm.
It reads mRNA and adds about 5–6 amino acids per second.
details: A human cell has millions (estimates around 10 million in fast-growing cells).
Two parts: a small (40S) and a large (60S) subunit.
At 1× speed you can watch the new chain grow at the real rate.

virtual_cell.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
summary: A lace of tubes and sheets spreading through the cell.
Makes proteins and fats, stores calcium.
details: Rough ER (with ribosomes) sits near the nucleus; smooth tubes reach out to the edge.
Tubes are about 50–100 nm wide and keep moving and re-joining.

virtual_cell.title: Golgi apparatus
summary: Stacks of flat sacs next to the nucleus: the post office.
It sorts, tags and packs proteins.
details: In human cells the stacks join into a ribbon of several µm near the centrosome.
Each stack has about 4–8 sacs (cisternae).
Cells that secrete a lot, like fibroblasts making collagen, have big Golgi.

virtual_cell.title: Vesicle
summary: A small bubble (50–100 nm) carrying cargo.
Motor proteins walk it along microtubules at about 1 µm per second.
details: Kinesin walks outwards (~0.8 µm/s), dynein inwards (~1 µm/s).
Off the track, a vesicle only jiggles slowly: the cytoplasm is very crowded.

virtual_cell.title: Mitochondrion
summary: The power station: makes ATP.
A tube about 0.5 µm wide and 1–10 µm long; a human cell has hundreds.
details: They form a network that splits and joins every few minutes.
The folds inside (cristae) hold ATP synthase, a spinning motor.
It has its own small DNA: it came from a bacterium long ago.

virtual_cell.title: ATP synthase
summary: A rotary motor about 10 nm wide in the cristae.
It spins over 100 times a second to make ATP.
details: Protons flowing through it turn the rotor.
Each turn makes 3 ATP.

virtual_cell.title: ATP
summary: The cell’s energy coin.
Made in mitochondria, spent everywhere.
details: A human body makes and recycles roughly its own weight in ATP every day.

virtual_cell.title: Lysosome
summary: A recycling bag full of enzymes, 0.1–1 µm.
A cell has a few hundred.
details: Its inside is acidic (pH about 4.5–5); a pump uses ATP to push protons in.
Its enzymes work best in acid, so any that leak into the near-neutral cytoplasm (pH ~7.2) do little harm.

virtual_cell.title: Peroxisome
summary: A small bag (0.1–0.5 µm) that burns fats.
It makes and destroys hydrogen peroxide.
details: Human cells have a few hundred.
Also helps make some special fats for the brain.

virtual_cell.title: Lipid droplet
summary: A store of fat, 0.5–2 µm.
Wrapped in a single layer of lipids.
details: Cells use them as an energy store and to make membranes.

virtual_cell.title: Centrosome
summary: Two tiny barrels (centrioles), 250 nm wide and 500 nm long.
Microtubules grow out from here.
details: Each barrel is 9 groups of 3 tubes.
In most human cells the older barrel also grows a primary cilium, a tiny antenna.
It helps pull chromosomes apart when the cell divides.

virtual_cell.title: Microtubule
summary: Hollow tubes 25 nm wide: roads and scaffolding.
Each tip grows ~12 µm/min, then suddenly shrinks.
details: This "dynamic instability" is simulated here with measured rates.
The bright tip is where new tubulin is added (biologists see it with EB1 tags).
Kinesin and dynein walk on them carrying cargo.

virtual_cell.title: Actin stress fibres
summary: Bundles of actin filaments (each 7 nm) running across the cell.
They pull on the ground like ropes.
details: They end at focal adhesions, the cell’s "feet".
A single filament is two strands twisted, crossing every 37 nm.

virtual_cell.title: Focal adhesion
summary: A cell’s “foot” that grips the surface, 1–5 µm long.
Stress fibres pull on it.
details: Made of integrins and many linking proteins.
Feet at the front form and mature in minutes.

virtual_cell.title: Vimentin filaments
summary: Rope-like filaments, 10 nm wide.
They cushion the nucleus and help the cell resist stretching.
details: Vimentin is the main intermediate filament of many cell types (e.g. fibroblasts); others use keratins.

virtual_cell.title: Vault
summary: A hollow barrel of protein and RNA, about 40 × 70 nm.
What it does is still not clear.
details: About 10,000 per cell (some cells have more).
Ideas include transport or defence, but no job is proven.

virtual_cell.title: Cytosol
summary: The gel that fills the cell: about 70% water.
Packed with roughly 3 million proteins per cubic µm.
details: So crowded that big things barely drift unless motors carry them.
Small molecules still diffuse fast: across the cell in seconds.

virtual_cell.title: Water molecule
summary: One oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms (H₂O).
About 99 of every 100 molecules in a cell are water.
details: Real water molecules jiggle and tumble trillions of times a second; here they are shown frozen or hugely slowed.
Water’s slightly charged ends help proteins fold.

virtual_cell.title: Glucose
summary: A sugar: a ring of carbon and oxygen.
Cells break it down for energy.
details: Glycolysis in the cytosol starts the job; mitochondria finish it and make ATP.

virtual_cell.title: Phospholipid
summary: A water-loving head and two oily tails, about 2.5 nm long.
Two layers of them make every membrane.
details: The tails hide from water, so lipids form two layers by themselves.
A kink in one tail keeps the membrane fluid.

virtual_cell.title: Base pair (DNA)
summary: Two DNA letters joined in the middle.
Each side hangs on a sugar-phosphate backbone.
details: A pairs with T, G pairs with C, held by weak hydrogen bonds.
Pairs are stacked 0.34 nm apart along the helix.

virtual_cell.title: Protein chain
summary: Amino acids linked in a chain by a ribosome.
The chain then folds into a working shape.
details: There are 20 kinds of amino acid; the gene sets their order.
The backbone repeats N–C–C; side chains stick out.

virtual_cell.title: Protein
summary: A folded chain of thousands of atoms, typically 3–10 nm.
Proteins do most of the work in a cell.
details: Enzymes, motors, pumps and scaffolds are all proteins.
Shown as simple blobs: real shapes are far more detailed.

virtual_cell.title: Hydrogen atom
summary: The smallest atom: 1 proton, 1 electron.
Made just after the Big Bang.
details: About 6 in 10 atoms in your body are hydrogen.

virtual_cell.title: Carbon atom
summary: 6 protons. The backbone of life’s molecules.
Made inside stars.
details: Carbon can bond to four other atoms, so it builds chains and rings.

virtual_cell.title: Nitrogen atom
summary: 7 protons.
Found in every amino acid and DNA letter.
details: Made inside stars (the CNO cycle).

virtual_cell.title: Oxygen atom
summary: 8 protons.
In water, sugars and the phosphate groups of ATP.
details: By mass, most of your body is oxygen (in water).

virtual_cell.title: Phosphorus atom
summary: 15 protons.
At the heart of ATP, DNA’s backbone and membrane lipids.
details: Made in massive stars and spread by supernovae.

virtual_cell.title: Electron cloud
summary: Electrons are not little planets.
The cloud shows where an electron is likely to be found.
details: This comes from quantum mechanics (orbitals).
An atom is almost all empty space.

virtual_cell.title: Atomic nucleus
summary: Protons and neutrons packed tight.
It holds over 99.9% of the atom’s mass.
details: Really about 100,000 times smaller than the atom; drawn far too big here.
Protons and neutrons are made of quarks.

virtual_body.title: Human body
summary: About 1.65 m tall here, close to the average adult height worldwide.
Made of about 30 trillion human cells.
details: Proportions follow standard adult measurements: the head is about 1/7.5 of the height, the navel about 60% of the way up.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Front view; one typical body, real people vary a lot.

virtual_body.title: Skin
summary: Your largest organ: about 1.6–1.8 m² and 3–4 kg.
It keeps water in and germs out.
details: Epidermis: about 0.1 mm thick (up to 1.5 mm on the soles).
Dermis: about 1–4 mm, with collagen made by fibroblast cells.
Under it is a fat layer (hypodermis) of varying thickness.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Shown as a smooth outline with no surface detail.

virtual_body.title: Face
summary: Eyes, nose, mouth and ears: most of the senses sit in the head, close to the brain.
details: The face has about 20 small muscles that make expressions.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simple outline, not a portrait.

virtual_body.title: Breast
summary: Made of fat, supporting tissue and the mammary gland, on top of the chest muscle (pectoralis major).
They develop at puberty; size and shape vary a lot between people and are not linked to how much milk they can make.
details: In pregnancy the breasts grow and prepare to make milk.
After birth they make milk to feed the baby.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simple contour lines, typical adult size.

virtual_body.title: Nipple and areola
summary: The nipple has several tiny openings (often about 5–10) where milk ducts end.
The darker ring around it is the areola, typically 3–6 cm across.
details: Small glands in the areola (Montgomery glands) keep the skin moist.
In pregnancy the areola often gets darker and larger; a newborn finds it more easily.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Drawn as plain circles.

virtual_body.title: Collarbone (clavicle)
summary: A long S-shaped bone you can see and feel under the skin, from the top of the breastbone to the shoulder.
It links the arm to the trunk.
details: It is the first bone to start hardening in a growing embryo, about 5–6 weeks after fertilisation.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Surface line only.

virtual_body.title: Knee (front)
summary: The kneecap (patella) sits in the tendon of the thigh muscle, in front of the knee joint.
It protects the joint and helps the thigh muscle straighten the leg.
details: The kneecap is still soft cartilage at birth and turns to bone at about 3–6 years old.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simple outline of the kneecap.

virtual_body.title: Mons pubis
summary: A rounded pad of fat over the pubic bone, at the front of the vulva.
It cushions the pubic bone; hair grows here after puberty (not drawn).
details: The creases at each side are the groin (inguinal) folds, where the thigh meets the trunk.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simple outline with light shading.

virtual_body.title: Navel (umbilicus)
summary: A scar where the umbilical cord was attached before birth.
details: In the womb the cord carried blood between the baby and the placenta: food and oxygen in, waste out.

virtual_body.title: Vulva (external genitals)
summary: The outer parts: the mons pubis, the outer and inner lips (labia majora and minora), the clitoris, and the separate openings of the urethra (for urine) and the vagina.
The labia protect the openings.
details: At birth the baby comes out through the vaginal opening, which stretches a great deal.
Shown here in a simple front view; much of it is hidden between the thighs when standing.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Simplified clinical outline; inner parts not drawn in detail.

virtual_body.title: Mammary glands
summary: Each breast has about 15–20 lobes. Each lobe has many small lobules that can make milk.
Ducts carry milk from the lobes to the nipple.
details: In pregnancy hormones (oestrogen, progesterone) grow the ducts and lobules.
After birth the hormone prolactin starts milk production; oxytocin squeezes milk out when the baby feeds (the let-down reflex).
virtual_body.drawing_note: Lobes and ducts drawn as a simple pattern.

virtual_body.title: Vagina
summary: A stretchy muscular tube about 7–10 cm long, from the cervix to the outside.
Menstrual blood leaves the body through it.
details: It is the birth canal: in childbirth it stretches to let the baby through.
Helpful bacteria (lactobacilli) keep it acidic, about pH 3.8–4.5, which protects against infection.
virtual_body.drawing_note: It runs up and backwards, so from the front it looks much shorter; shown over the bladder so you can see it.

virtual_body.title: Cervix
summary: The narrow lower end of the uterus, about 2.5–3 cm long, opening into the vagina.
It makes mucus that changes through the monthly cycle.
details: In pregnancy it stays closed with a mucus plug that protects the baby.
In labour it opens (dilates) to about 10 cm so the baby can be born.

virtual_body.title: Fallopian tubes
summary: Two tubes about 10–12 cm long from the uterus towards the ovaries.
Their finger-like ends catch the egg when it is released.
details: Fertilisation (egg meets sperm) usually happens inside the tube.
Tiny hairs (cilia) move the early embryo to the uterus over about 3–5 days.

virtual_body.title: Skull
summary: 22 bones; 8 make the braincase around the brain.
The jaw (mandible) is the only one that moves.
details: Adult skull is about 18–20 cm from front to back.

virtual_body.title: Spine (vertebral column)
summary: 33 vertebrae: 7 neck, 12 chest, 5 lower back, then the fused sacrum (5) and tailbone (about 4).
It holds the spinal cord.
details: In an adult woman it is about 60–70 cm long.
Seen from the front it is mostly hidden behind the organs.

virtual_body.title: Rib cage
summary: 12 pairs of ribs. The top 7 join the breastbone (sternum) directly.
Pairs 11 and 12 float free at the front.
details: It protects the heart and lungs and moves with every breath.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Rib curves simplified.

virtual_body.title: Sternum (breastbone)
summary: A flat bone about 15–17 cm long in the middle of the chest.
details: Three parts: manubrium, body and the small xiphoid process.

virtual_body.title: Clavicle (collarbone)
summary: Joins the breastbone to the shoulder blade.
About 14–15 cm long in women.
details: One of the most commonly broken bones.

virtual_body.title: Humerus
summary: The upper arm bone, about 30 cm long in women.
details: Its round head fits the shallow shoulder socket, so the shoulder moves a lot but dislocates easily.

virtual_body.title: Radius and ulna
summary: The two forearm bones. The radius is on the thumb side.
The radius turns around the ulna to rotate your palm.
details: About 22–25 cm long.

virtual_body.title: Hand bones
summary: 27 bones: 8 wrist bones (carpals), 5 metacarpals, 14 finger bones (phalanges).
details: Both hands together hold over a quarter of the body’s bones.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Wrist bones shown as one group.

virtual_body.title: Pelvis
summary: Two hip bones plus the sacrum, forming a ring.
In women it is wider and rounder, making room for childbirth.
details: The female pelvic inlet is oval and wide; the angle under the pubic bones is usually over 80°.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Outline simplified.

virtual_body.title: Femur (thigh bone)
summary: The longest and strongest bone: about 42–45 cm in a 1.65 m adult (about 26–27% of height).
details: It slants inward to the knee; the slant is larger in women because the pelvis is wider.

virtual_body.title: Patella (kneecap)
summary: A bone that grows inside the tendon of the thigh muscle.
details: About 5 cm across.

virtual_body.title: Tibia and fibula
summary: The shin bone (tibia) carries the weight; the thin fibula is on the outside.
details: The tibia is about 35–37 cm long in women.

virtual_body.title: Foot bones
summary: 26 bones: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges.
details: Seen from the front, the foot is foreshortened.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Foot shown foreshortened and simplified.

virtual_body.title: Brain
summary: About 1.2–1.3 kg in adult women, with about 86 billion neurons.
Uses about 20% of the body’s energy.
details: How it makes thoughts and feelings is still being worked out.

virtual_body.title: Eye
summary: About 24 mm across.
The retina has about 120 million rods and 6 million cones.

virtual_body.title: Thyroid gland
summary: A butterfly-shaped gland in the neck, about 5 cm wide.
Its hormones set how fast the body uses energy.

virtual_body.title: Lungs
summary: The right lung has 3 lobes, the left has 2 and a notch for the heart.
About 300–500 million air sacs (alveoli).
details: At rest you breathe about 12–16 times a minute, about 0.5 L each time.
Their inner surface is about 50–75 m².

virtual_body.title: Heart
summary: About the size of a fist, 250–300 g in women.
Beats about 60–100 times a minute; shown at 70.
details: Pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute at rest.
It sits in the middle of the chest, tilted to the person’s left.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Outline simplified. Zoom in to see the 4 chambers and 4 valves (textbook cut-away).

virtual_body.title: Right atrium
summary: Collects oxygen-poor blood from the body through the two venae cavae.
Holds the sinoatrial node, the heart’s natural pacemaker.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Right ventricle
summary: Pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs through the pulmonary valve.
Wall about 3–5 mm thick; pressure about 25 mmHg when it squeezes.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Left atrium
summary: Collects oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through 4 pulmonary veins.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Left ventricle
summary: Pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body through the aorta.
Thickest wall, about 1 cm; pressure about 120 mmHg when it squeezes.
details: About 70 mL leaves it each beat at rest.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Septum
summary: The wall between the left and right sides, so the two bloods do not mix.
details: Carries the electrical bundle that makes the ventricles squeeze together.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Tricuspid valve
summary: 3 flaps between the right atrium and right ventricle.
Shown opening while the ventricle fills, shutting when it squeezes.
details: Its closing (with the mitral valve) is the first heart sound, “lub”.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Mitral valve
summary: 2 flaps between the left atrium and left ventricle.
Shown opening while the ventricle fills, shutting when it squeezes.
details: Its closing (with the tricuspid) is the first heart sound, “lub”.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Pulmonary valve
summary: 3 half-moon flaps from the right ventricle to the lungs’ artery.
Shown opening when the ventricle squeezes.
details: Its closing (with the aortic valve) is the second heart sound, “dub”.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Aortic valve
summary: 3 half-moon flaps from the left ventricle into the aorta.
Shown opening when the ventricle squeezes.
details: Its closing (with the pulmonary valve) is the second heart sound, “dub”.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Textbook cut-away (coronal section), simplified. In real life the right ventricle faces the front and the left atrium sits at the back.

virtual_body.title: Liver
summary: The largest internal organ, about 1.2–1.5 kg.
Mostly on the person’s right, under the ribs.
details: Does over 500 jobs, from cleaning blood to making bile.

virtual_body.title: Gallbladder
summary: A small bag under the liver that stores bile, about 50 mL.

virtual_body.title: Stomach
summary: J-shaped, on the person’s left under the ribs.
Holds about 1–1.5 L after a meal.
details: Its acid has a pH of about 1.5–3.5.

virtual_body.title: Spleen
summary: About 11 cm long, on the person’s left behind the stomach.
Filters old red blood cells and helps fight infection.

virtual_body.title: Pancreas
summary: About 15 cm long, behind the stomach.
Makes digestive juices and insulin.

virtual_body.title: Kidneys
summary: Two bean shapes about 11 cm long at the back of the belly.
Together they filter about 180 L of blood plasma a day.
details: The right kidney usually sits a little lower, under the liver.

virtual_body.title: Small intestine
summary: About 3–5 m long in a living person.
Where most food is absorbed.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Coils drawn as a simplified pattern, not each real loop.

virtual_body.title: Large intestine
summary: About 1.5 m long, framing the small intestine.
Takes water back and holds trillions of gut bacteria.

virtual_body.title: Bladder
summary: Stores urine: usually 300–500 mL.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Drawn see-through so the reproductive organs behind it show.

virtual_body.title: Uterus
summary: A pear-shaped muscular organ about 7–8 cm long, behind and above the bladder.
Each month its lining thickens; if there is no pregnancy, the lining is shed as a period.
details: In pregnancy the early embryo implants in the lining and the placenta forms.
The uterus grows from about 60 g to about 1 kg and holds the baby for about 40 weeks.
In labour its strong muscle contracts to push the baby out.

virtual_body.title: Ovaries
summary: Two almond-sized glands, about 3–4 cm long, either side of the uterus.
They hold the eggs and make the hormones oestrogen and progesterone.
details: A baby girl is born with about 1–2 million immature eggs; only about 400–500 are released in a lifetime, usually one a month.
After an egg is released, the corpus luteum makes progesterone, which supports an early pregnancy.

virtual_body.title: Skeletal muscles
summary: About 600 muscles, roughly 30–35% of body weight in women.
They pull on bones through tendons.
details: Only the larger surface muscles are drawn.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Main surface muscles only, shapes simplified.

virtual_body.title: Deltoid
summary: The rounded shoulder muscle; lifts the arm sideways.

virtual_body.title: Pectoralis major
summary: The large fan-shaped chest muscle; pulls the arm forward and across.

virtual_body.title: Biceps brachii
summary: Bends the elbow and turns the palm up.

virtual_body.title: Forearm muscles
summary: About 20 muscles that move the wrist and fingers.

virtual_body.title: Rectus abdominis
summary: The long belly muscle, split into sections by bands of tendon.

virtual_body.title: External oblique
summary: The side belly muscle; twists and bends the trunk.

virtual_body.title: Sternocleidomastoid
summary: The neck muscle that turns and tilts the head.

virtual_body.title: Quadriceps
summary: Four muscles at the front of the thigh that straighten the knee.
details: One of the strongest muscle groups in the body.

virtual_body.title: Sartorius
summary: The longest muscle in the body, crossing the thigh diagonally.

virtual_body.title: Adductors
summary: Inner-thigh muscles that pull the legs together.

virtual_body.title: Tibialis anterior
summary: Lifts the front of the foot.

virtual_body.title: Gastrocnemius (calf)
summary: The calf muscle; lifts the heel through the Achilles tendon.

virtual_body.title: Arteries
summary: Carry blood away from the heart (red here).
The aorta is about 2.5–3 cm wide.
details: Blood in the aorta moves on average about 20 cm/s; the moving dots use that speed.
All arteries together are roughly 9,000–19,000 km long (newer estimates); the old "100,000 km" figure counts every vessel and is too high.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Main arteries are mapped; the small branches that appear as you zoom are a generated pattern, not a map.

virtual_body.title: Aorta
summary: The biggest artery, about 2.5–3 cm wide.
It arches over the heart and runs down in front of the spine.
details: It splits into the two iliac arteries at about the navel.

virtual_body.title: Veins
summary: Carry blood back to the heart (blue here; real blood is always red, darker in veins).
details: Valves stop blood falling back down the legs.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Main veins drawn; small branches are a generated pattern.

virtual_body.title: Nerves
summary: Nerves carry signals between the brain, spinal cord and body.
Fast nerve signals travel up to about 120 m/s.
details: The moving dots are shown much slower than real so you can see them.
virtual_body.drawing_note: Main nerves drawn; small branches are a generated pattern. Signals slowed down.

virtual_body.title: Spinal cord
summary: About 43 cm long in women; ends near the first lumbar vertebra.
Below that, nerve roots continue as the "horse’s tail" (cauda equina).

virtual_body.title: Sciatic nerve
summary: The thickest nerve, up to about 2 cm wide, running down the back of the thigh.
details: Seen from the front it lies behind the femur.

virtual_body.title: Arm nerves
summary: The median, ulnar and radial nerves run down the arm to the hand.
Hitting the ulnar nerve at the elbow is the "funny bone".

planet.title: Earth
summary: Radius about 6,371 km. Mass about 6 × 10²⁴ kg.
Formed about 4.54 billion years ago.
details: Drawn as a cut-away: real layers to scale, shapes simplified (land on the left half, ocean on the right).

planet.title: Exosphere
summary: From about 600 km up to about 10,000 km.
Gas so thin its atoms hardly ever meet.
details: Its outer edge is fuzzy; it fades into space (some count it out to the Moon).

planet.title: Thermosphere
summary: From about 85 to 600 km up. Auroras glow here.
The ISS flies here, about 400 km up.
details: Thin gas can reach 2,000 °C, but it would feel cold: too few atoms to warm you.

planet.title: Mesosphere
summary: From about 50 to 85 km up.
Most meteors burn up here.
details: The coldest part of the atmosphere, about −90 °C at the top.

planet.title: Stratosphere
summary: From about 12 to 50 km up.
Holds the ozone layer, which blocks most UV light.

planet.title: Troposphere
summary: From the ground up to about 12 km (8 km at the poles, 18 km at the equator).
Almost all weather happens here.
details: Holds about three quarters of the air’s mass.

planet.title: Atmosphere
summary: A thin layer of gas: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen.
Zoom in to see its 5 layers.
details: Half of all air is below about 5.5 km.

planet.title: Kármán line
summary: 100 km up: a common agreed edge of space.
It is a convention, not a physical wall.

planet.title: Space Station (ISS)
summary: Orbits about 400–420 km up.
Goes round Earth about every 90 minutes.
details: Shown far bigger than real (it is about 109 m wide).

planet.title: Ocean
summary: Covers about 71% of Earth. Average depth about 3.7 km.
Deepest point: about 10.9 km (Challenger Deep).

planet.title: Oceanic crust
summary: About 7 km thick, mostly basalt.
Young: rarely older than about 200 million years.
details: Made at mid-ocean ridges and sinks back into the mantle.

planet.title: Continental crust
summary: About 35 km thick on average, up to 70 km under big mountains.
Lighter granite-like rock; parts are over 4 billion years old.
details: Its base is the Moho, where rock gets much denser.

planet.title: Crust
summary: Earth’s thin rocky skin: less than 1% of its volume.
Zoom in to see ocean and continent crust.

planet.title: Upper mantle
summary: From the crust down to about 410 km. Solid rock (peridotite).
It flows very slowly, a few cm a year, moving the plates.
details: The plates (lithosphere) are the stiff top ~100 km; below is the softer asthenosphere.

planet.title: Transition zone
summary: From about 410 to 660 km down. Minerals squeeze into new forms.
It may hold a lot of water inside minerals (how much is still debated).
details: A diamond found in 2014 held ringwoodite with water, from this zone.

planet.title: Lower mantle
summary: From about 660 to 2,891 km down. Hot solid rock.
Its main mineral, bridgmanite, is the most common mineral on Earth.
details: Two continent-sized blobs sit at its base; where they came from is unknown.

planet.title: Outer core
summary: From about 2,891 to 5,150 km down. Liquid iron and nickel.
Its flow makes Earth’s magnetic field.

planet.title: Inner core
summary: A solid iron-nickel ball, radius about 1,220 km.
About 5,000–5,400 °C, near the Sun’s surface temperature.
details: It is solid because of the huge pressure.
Its age is debated: roughly 0.5–1.5 billion years.

L.name: Dying low-mass stars
L.note: Giant stars (1–8 Suns) catch neutrons slowly (s-process), then puff off their outer layers. (Most of our lithium: such stars and novae.)

M.name: Exploding massive stars
M.note: Fusion in stars >8 Suns, spread by core-collapse supernovae.

W.name: Exploding white dwarfs
W.note: Type Ia supernovae: lots of iron-group metals.

N.name: Merging neutron stars
N.note: Rapid neutron catching (r-process). Maybe also rare supernovae (debated).

R.name: Radioactive decay only
R.note: No long-lived form; made as other elements decay.

H.name: Human-made
H.note: Made in reactors or accelerators (some also in traces or in stars, briefly).
